title: Black Cannabis Pioneers: A Black History Month Guide

body:
Black cannabis pioneers include the advocates who challenged unequal enforcement, the entrepreneurs who opened early licensed businesses, and the doctors and scientists who brought evidence and equity into the debate. Their stories belong in Black History Month because the burden of prohibition never fell evenly. Below, meet four of them, see how equity programs and record clearing work, and find practical ways to support Black-owned cannabis businesses in Michigan and beyond.

## Why February matters in cannabis

For decades, marijuana enforcement landed hardest on Black communities. The ACLU's 2020 analysis of arrest data found that in 2018, Black people were 3.64 times more likely than white people to be arrested for marijuana possession. Use rates, meanwhile, were about the same for both groups. In 2018 alone, police made nearly 700,000 marijuana arrests, which made up over 43% of the country's drug arrests.

Public health researchers at George Washington University describe how that harsh enforcement fed high incarceration, economic hardship and social inequities among racial and ethnic minority and low-income communities. Those harms have outlasted the old laws. For the longer history of the drug war itself, read our companion piece on [Black History Month and cannabis prohibition](/blog/celebrating-black-history-month/).

## Black cannabis pioneers: advocates, entrepreneurs, physicians and scientists

Many Black leaders have shaped legal cannabis. These four show how wide that work runs, from policy and business to medicine and research.

### Kassandra Frederique, policy advocate

When Kassandra Frederique testified before a U.S. House subcommittee in 2021, her filed biography listed her as executive director of the Drug Policy Alliance, a national nonprofit working to end the war on drugs. It also says she designed the campaign behind a drop of more than 99% in New York City marijuana arrests since 2010. Racial justice runs through her campaigns on policing, overdoses and legalization, and she has pushed for repair for the communities the drug war harmed most.

### Wanda James, entrepreneur

Wanda James is a Colorado entrepreneur who now serves on the University of Colorado Board of Regents. Her university biography says that in 2009 she and her husband, chef Scott Durrah, became the first African Americans to own a cannabis company in America. It also lists four years of military service and jobs at two Fortune 100 companies. Her election to the board made her the first Black woman elected to it in over 44 years.

### Dr. Rachel Knox, physician

Dr. Rachel Knox trained in family, integrative and functional medicine and went on to specialize in cannabinoid medicine. In February 2021 testimony to a Kansas House committee, she spoke as a board member of Doctors for Cannabis Regulation, a physician group focused on sound cannabis regulation. She also described chairing the governor-appointed Oregon Cannabis Commission. Her recommendations included required cannabis training for health professionals and a medical program that puts research and health equity first.

### Dr. Carl Hart, scientist

Dr. Carl Hart, a professor of psychology at Columbia University, studies how drugs affect the mind and body. His book *Drug Use for Grown-Ups* takes aim at current drug laws. Speaking with Columbia Magazine, he argued that those laws are wielded most harshly against Black people and the poor.

Plenty of other names belong here, including small-brand founders and the budtenders, growers and lab staff whose work rarely makes the news. Our feature on [women in cannabis](/blog/women-in-cannabis/) profiles more leaders.

## Building a business: capital, licensing and other barriers

A licensed cannabis business needs money, real estate, compliance know-how and patience, usually long before the first sale. The George Washington University team notes that entrepreneurs from hard-hit communities remain underrepresented across the industry, partly because of limited business experience or limited money to start with.

Timing mattered too. In Colorado and Washington, equity programs arrived long after legalization, and the researchers say that delay may have produced uneven business opportunities in the first years of legal sales. Federal law adds complications for every cannabis company; our [rescheduling explainer](/blog/cannabis-rescheduling/) follows the federal picture as of October 2026.

Founders have found different ways around these barriers:

- **State equity support.** Some states offer training, grants or loans. Colorado's Cannabis Business Office, for example, has made loans to equity licensees for seed capital and running costs such as rent and application fees.
- **Trade groups.** The [Minority Cannabis Business Association](https://minoritycannabis.org/), a national trade association for minority cannabis entrepreneurs, advocates for equity-focused policies, hosts educational events and helps business owners build networks.

## Social equity programs explained, and Michigan's approach

Social equity programs try to widen access to the legal market for the people and places prohibition hit hardest. A 2025 case study of five states describes these efforts as combining three things: criminal justice reform, help for equity entrepreneurs and reinvestment of cannabis revenue in affected communities.

For would-be business owners, the help usually includes some mix of:

- **Eligibility rules** tied to a past cannabis arrest or conviction, years spent living in a disproportionately impacted area, or income limits.
- **Set-aside licenses**, either reserved for equity applicants or created just for them.
- **Training and technical help**, from accelerator programs to tracks built for specific roles.
- **Financial help** such as grants, loans or fee waivers, which varies a lot from state to state.

Because approaches differ and the evidence base is still small, the researchers call for ongoing evaluation of what works. How Michigan handles equity licensing, including who qualifies and what help is offered, is covered in our [social equity explainer](/blog/cannabis-social-equity/). Program details change, so check there and on our [Michigan cannabis law page](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) for the state's rules as of October 2026.

## Expungement in Michigan: clearing past cannabis convictions

A cannabis conviction can keep turning up in background checks long after a sentence ends, at job interviews, on rental applications and beyond. Expungement and sealing limit who can see an old record, while a pardon offers forgiveness of a different kind.

The same 2025 study counts 24 states that had legalized adult use as of March 2025. Every one of them, plus Washington, D.C., had laws creating some pathway to expunge, pardon, seal or annul low-level cannabis convictions. Which offenses qualify, and how the process works, differs from state to state.

For the process here, our guide to [Michigan marijuana expungement](/blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/) explains who may qualify and where to begin. Wherever you live, a few steps help:

1. Request a copy of your criminal record, so you know exactly which convictions, courts and dates are involved.
2. Talk with a lawyer or a legal aid group before you file anything.
3. Keep copies of every form, receipt and court notice.

## Finding and supporting Black-owned cannabis brands and businesses

Supporting Black-owned cannabis businesses starts with knowing who stands behind what you buy:

- **Ask at the counter.** At High Society, a budtender can talk you through the brands on your store's menu. Then visit a brand's own website to see who founded it and who owns it today.
- **Look at ownership, not just the origin story.** Investments and sales can change who owns a company, so a founding story from years ago may not describe the business now.
- **Follow equity-minded trade groups.** Groups for minority cannabis entrepreneurs, such as the Minority Cannabis Business Association, host events and share policy news. Following them is an easy way to learn who is building in the industry.
- **Buy, review and recommend.** Choose products you enjoy, leave honest reviews and tell other adults 21 and older about them.

## Keeping it going after February: community groups and education

February is a beginning, not a finish line. A few ways to keep learning and helping all year:

- **Read and listen.** Dr. Hart's books and the Drug Policy Alliance's online resource library are solid places to begin on drug policy.
- **Support community groups.** Look for nonprofits working on clemency, reentry, record clearing and voter education, and look into a group's track record before you give.
- **Show up locally.** Local governments often decide where cannabis businesses can open, so attend city or township meetings when cannabis is on the agenda, and vote in local elections.
- **Share the history.** Juneteenth and Black History Month are natural moments to talk about who bore the brunt of cannabis enforcement, and what fairer rules could look like.

21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Why is Black History Month important to the cannabis industry?
faq.a: Because prohibition's burden fell unevenly. In the ACLU's 2020 analysis, the likelihood of a possession arrest in 2018 was 3.64 times higher for Black people than for white people, despite similar marijuana use in both groups. The month is a chance to recognize the advocates, founders, doctors and scientists who pushed for a fairer legal market, and to support work that isn't finished yet, from equity licensing to clearing old records.

faq.q: What is a cannabis social equity program?
faq.a: It's a state or local effort to open the legal cannabis market to the people most affected by prohibition. Programs often pair record relief with help for equity entrepreneurs and reinvestment in hard-hit communities. Business support can include set-aside licenses, training, and grants, loans or fee waivers. Eligibility is often tied to a past cannabis conviction, where you've lived or your income, and the details vary widely by state.

faq.q: How can I find Black-owned cannabis brands in Michigan?
faq.a: Start by asking a budtender about the brands on your store's menu, then check each brand's own website to see who founded it and who owns it now, since ownership can change. Trade groups for minority cannabis entrepreneurs, such as the Minority Cannabis Business Association, are another way to learn who's building in the industry. When you find a brand you like, buying it, reviewing it and recommending it all help.

review.notes: Fact-check 2026-10-24: 25 claims checked, 7 fixed (1 wrong, 2 unsupported, 4 overstated). All 6 sources re-opened and support the text (Columbia Magazine via curl). Hart's current Columbia title verified on the psychology department page and the sentence made title-neutral rather than adding a 7th source. Writer's notes: Michigan social equity and expungement specifics are not in facts/law-facts.json, so the article points to /blog/cannabis-social-equity/, /blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/ and /cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/ instead of stating Michigan rules. No High Society equity, donation, event or partnership claims. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): The ACLU's 2020 report (A Tale of Two Countries, PDF Table 6, read 2026-10-24) gives 3.31 for 2010 and 3.64 for 2018: 3.64 is the 2018 ratio, not a 2010-2018 average, so the year is now stated.
